cim: Survey Finds Twenty-Two Percent of Forensic Practitioners Use Generative AI

szoveg_eredeti:
Survey Finds Twenty-Two Percent of Forensic Practitioners Use Generative AI

Nearly one in four forensic medicine professionals has utilized generative artificial intelligence at least once within a professional capacity, according to a recent international survey. Although automated generative platforms have achieved widespread visibility since late 2022, their practical application within medicolegal environments remains emerging, unstandardized, and largely informal rather than serving as routine or formally regulated clinical practice.

The study sought to document both private and professional perceptions and uses of generative tools across global forensic medicine practitioners, examining junior and senior specialists alike. While practitioner deployment of non-generative artificial intelligence was first formally documented in 2024, baseline information concerning how generative models are handled in professional contexts, whether through informal workplace experimentation or explicit institutional regulation, had remained unrecorded.

To address this evidence gap, researchers administered a focused online survey open from November 1, 2024, through March 15, 2025. The survey gathered 121 completed responses from practitioners across multiple regions. Geographically, Europe constituted the vast majority of the participant pool at 74 percent, followed by the Middle East at 14 percent, Asia at 8 percent, and Africa at 4 percent.

Demographic assessments revealed a participant sex ratio of 0.6 among responding professionals. In terms of professional seniority, the ratio of resident trainees to senior practitioners stood at 0.8, providing a structured comparison between early-career specialists and experienced staff. Across the overall sample, self-reported knowledge regarding generative artificial intelligence proved to be considerably lower than practitioner familiarity with established non-generative systems.

In terms of workplace implementation, 22 percent of practitioners reported employing generative tools at least once in their professional activities. Nevertheless, the investigators highlighted that such engagements do not represent an established norm, standard operating protocol, or regulated procedure at this stage. Instead, current utilization reflects sporadic, individual engagement rather than institutionalized adoption within forensic healthcare settings.

Participant perspectives regarding prospective utility indicated a prevailing consensus that generative artificial intelligence could likely offer valuable support over the medium term. Crucially, respondents maintained that any meaningful forensic application would strictly mandate ongoing oversight and active supervision by qualified practitioners. Furthermore, resident physicians proved consistently more reserved across every evaluated technological domain when contrasted with their more senior counterparts.

Overall, the empirical findings demonstrate that technology adoption in forensic medicine is moving far less rapidly than portrayed by numerous media accounts and select scientific publications. Given the swift evolution of the computational landscape, the study authors underscored that systematic monitoring will be essential moving forward, particularly alongside the phased implementation of the European Union AI Act.

Subject of Research: Perceptions and professional adoption of generative artificial intelligence in forensic medicine

Article Title: Generative artificial intelligence and forensic medicine professionals: knowledge, representations and uses in 2024-25. A short international survey

Article References: Lefèvre, T., Laugier, V., Tournois, L., & Ludes, B. (2026). Generative artificial intelligence and forensic medicine professionals: knowledge, representations and uses in 2024-25. A short international survey. International Journal of Legal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00414-026-04094-4

Keywords: forensic medicine, generative artificial intelligence, non-generative artificial intelligence, international survey, medical residents, senior practitioners, professional adoption, clinical supervision, European Union AI Act, informal workplace use, regulated medical practice, practitioner perceptions, legal medicine, technology adoption rates, physician demographics, digital forensic tools

News Source: Ophelia Keating. (November 23, 2026). Survey Finds Twenty-Two Percent of Forensic Practitioners Use Generative AI. Scienmag.
